original_summary: A nervous narrator insists he is not mad, only over-sensitive: his hearing is so sharp, he says, that he hears all things in heaven and in hell. He loves the old man he lives with, who has never wronged him and whose gold he does not want, but he cannot bear the old man's pale blue 'vulture eye' with a film over it, and he decides to kill him to be free of it. For seven nights, exactly at midnight, he opens the old man's door very slowly, slides in a closed dark lantern, and lets one thin ray fall on the eye; the eye is always shut, so he cannot do it, and each morning he speaks warmly to the old man. On the eighth night his thumb slips on the lantern's fastening, the old man sits up and cries 'Who's there?', and the narrator stays motionless in the dark for a whole hour while the old man sits listening, afraid. When the narrator at last opens a crack of light and it falls on the wide-open vulture eye, he hears a low, dull, quick sound like a watch wrapped in cotton, the old man's heart, growing louder and louder; fearing a neighbour will hear it, he leaps in with a yell, drags the old man to the floor, and pulls the heavy bed over him; the heart beats on until it stops. He hides the body under three planks of the floor so cleverly that there is no stain or blood. At four o'clock, three police officers knock: a neighbour heard a shriek. The narrator, calm, welcomes them, says the shriek was his own in a dream and the old man is away in the country, and takes them through the house; in his confidence he sets chairs in the old man's room and seats himself on the very spot above the hidden body. The officers are satisfied and chat, but the narrator grows pale, his ears ring, and he begins to hear the low, quick sound again, louder and louder, which the officers seem not to hear. He talks faster and louder, paces, raves, grates his chair on the boards, convinced they hear it and are mocking him with their smiles, until he cannot bear it and shrieks, 'Villains! dissemble no more! I admit the deed! Tear up the planks! Here, here! It is the beating of his hideous heart!'
seed_elements: A narrator who speaks directly to a listener ('you') opens by insisting he is not mad: he is only very, very nervous, and the illness has sharpened his senses, above all his hearing. He asks the listener to hear how calmly and healthily he can tell the whole story.

He says he loved the old man, who never wronged or insulted him, and he did not want the old man's gold. It was the eye: a pale blue eye with a film over it, like a vulture's. Whenever it fell on him his blood ran cold, and little by little he decided to kill the old man and be rid of the eye for ever.

He argues that a madman could not have been so wise: he was never kinder to the old man than in the week before the deed. Every night at about midnight he turned the latch, opened the door very slowly, put in a dark lantern shut tight, then his head, then let one thin ray fall on the eye. For seven nights the eye was always closed, so he could not do the work, because it was the Evil Eye, not the old man, that troubled him. Every morning he went in boldly and spoke warmly to the old man, asking how he had slept.

On the eighth night he is more careful than ever and feels proud of his own cunning; he even chuckles, and the old man moves in bed. In the pitch-dark room he keeps pushing the door open. Then his thumb slips on the tin fastening of the lantern, the old man sits up and cries out, 'Who's there?', and the narrator keeps perfectly still, saying nothing, for a whole hour, while the old man sits listening in the dark.

The narrator hears a slight groan and knows it is the groan of mortal terror, a sound he knows from his own nights. He pities the old man while chuckling inside, and imagines him telling himself it is only the wind in the chimney or a mouse or a cricket, all in vain, because Death has stalked before him.

At last the narrator opens a tiny crevice in the lantern and a single thin ray, like a spider's thread, falls full on the vulture eye, which is wide open. His fury grows. Then he hears a low, dull, quick sound, like a watch wrapped in cotton: the beating of the old man's heart. It grows quicker and louder every moment, and the narrator, himself in terror, fears a neighbour will hear it.

With a loud yell he throws open the lantern and leaps into the room. The old man shrieks once. The narrator drags him to the floor and pulls the heavy bed over him. The heart goes on beating, muffled, for many minutes, then stops. He examines the body: stone dead, no pulsation. The eye will trouble him no more.

Proud of his caution, he hides the body under three planks taken up from the floor of the chamber and replaces them so cleverly that no eye could see anything wrong; there is no stain, no blood-spot. It is four o'clock when a knocking comes at the street door. Three men enter and say they are police officers: a neighbour heard a shriek in the night, and they have been sent to search the house.

The narrator, with a light heart, welcomes them. He says the shriek was his own, in a dream, and the old man is away in the country. He shows them through the whole house, even the old man's room and his treasures, brings chairs into the room, and, in the wild audacity of his triumph, sets his own seat on the very spot above the hidden body.

The officers are satisfied and chat of ordinary things, but the narrator grows pale and his head aches; he feels a ringing in his ears that becomes more distinct until he understands that the noise is not inside his ears. It is the same low, dull, quick sound. He talks faster and louder, argues about trifles, paces, raves, swears, and grates his chair upon the boards, but the noise rises over everything and grows louder, louder, louder, while the men go on chatting pleasantly and smiling.

He decides they hear it, they suspect, they know, and they are mocking his horror; he cannot bear their smiles any longer and feels he must scream or die. He shrieks, 'Villains! dissemble no more! I admit the deed! Tear up the planks! Here, here! It is the beating of his hideous heart!'
discarded_elements: The repeated arguments that he is wise and cunning ('would a madman have been so wise?'), if space is needed, and the repeated assurances 'you would have laughed to see how cunningly I thrust it in'
The long description of the old man's imagined thoughts (wind in the chimney, a mouse, a cricket) and the personification of Death with his black shadow, if space is needed
The graphic detail of how the body was dealt with beyond one plain statement that he hid the body under the floorboards

The detail of the 'death watches in the wall', the narrator's explanation of the groan as the sound of his own past terrors, and the exact wording of the officers' introduction and the neighbour's report, if space is needed
conversion_plan: Keep the original's night-time house, the first-person voice and the original order of events; do not modernize the setting, do not change the narrator into a third person, and do not add any new character, motive, explanation or supernatural event. Write it in clear, natural English at about 400 words as a short horror monologue whose fear comes from the narrator's calm, over-confident voice and from sound and silence: the latch, the thin ray of light, the old man's cry, the long silence, the low quick beating like a watch wrapped in cotton, the knock at the door, the officers' chatting. Use short, concrete sentences; let the narrator keep addressing the listener ('you', 'you fancy me mad'); keep his insistence that he is not mad and that his hearing is sharp, because that claim is the heart of the story. Neither the narrator nor the old man nor the officers have personal names: refer to them as I, the old man, and the officers (the police), exactly as the original does. Preserve the central events in order and the cause-and-effect chain: the narrator, who insists he is calm and not mad, is driven only by the old man's pale blue 'vulture eye' and not by money or hatred; for seven nights at midnight he looks in with a single thin ray of light but the eye is always closed; on the eighth night the old man wakes, cries 'Who's there?' and sits listening in terror while the narrator stays still; when the ray falls on the open eye the narrator hears the old man's heart beating louder and louder, fears a neighbour will hear, rushes in, kills the old man and hides the body under the floorboards, leaving no trace; three officers come because a neighbour heard a shriek, and the narrator calmly shows them the house and even sits above the hiding place; as they chat he hears the low, quick beating again, louder and louder, which the officers do not seem to hear; unable to bear it, certain they are mocking him, he screams that he did it and tells them to tear up the planks. Keep the ending exactly as the original leaves it: the story ends on the narrator's confession, with no aftermath, no arrest, no explanation of whether the sound was real or only in his mind, and no moral or comment of your own. Do not describe the body in graphic detail: the hiding of the body beneath the floor may be told in one plain, calm sentence. Do not reveal before the right moment that the narrator will confess, or that the sound in the last scene is the heartbeat again; do not add sound-effect words. Compress by trimming the narrator's repeated arguments that he is wise, the old man's imagined thoughts and the details of the cleaning up, not by cutting the vulture eye, the seven midnight nights, the eighth night, the heartbeat, the killing, the hiding under the floor, the officers, the sound that grows or the confession.

title: 告げ口心臓 The Tell-Tale Heart (Edgar Allan Poe)

ending_reveal.meaning: The narrator, who has insisted all along that he is calm and sane, sits above the floorboards where he hid the old man's body while the officers chat. He hears the low, quick beating again, louder and louder, which the officers do not seem to hear; he decides they know and are mocking him, cannot bear it, and screams that he did the deed and that they must tear up the planks, because it is the beating of the old man's hideous heart. The story ends on that confession, with no aftermath and no explanation of whether the sound was real or only in his mind.
ending_reveal.source_quote: It is the beating of his hideous heart!
ending_reveal.withhold_until_end: Before the final scene, do not hint that the narrator will confess, that the officers will not hear the sound, or that the sound in the last scene is the heartbeat again; do not explain the ending, say whether the sound was real or imagined, mention an arrest or any aftermath, or add a moral or comment.

setups_and_payoffs.setup: The narrator claims his senses are over-acute and that he hears all things in heaven and earth, so he is not mad, and he asks the listener to judge how calmly he tells the story
setups_and_payoffs.payoff: In the last scene he alone hears the low, quick heartbeat of the dead man, louder and louder, and is driven to confess

setups_and_payoffs.setup: The old man's pale blue 'vulture eye' is the only reason for the killing; it is closed on seven midnights, so the narrator cannot act
setups_and_payoffs.payoff: On the eighth night the ray of light falls on the wide-open eye and the heartbeat begins, and the narrator kills the old man

key_roles.role: the narrator, the unnamed first-person speaker who insists he is sane, kills the old man and finally confesses
the old man, the narrator's housemate whose pale blue vulture eye the narrator cannot bear, who is killed on the eighth night
the three police officers who come at four in the morning, are welcomed and shown the house, and sit chatting above the hidden body

key_causality: The narrator, obsessed with the old man's vulture eye, looks in on seven midnights but the eye is always closed; on the eighth night the old man wakes and sits listening in terror, the ray falls on the open eye, the narrator hears the heart beat louder and louder and, afraid a neighbour will hear it, kills the old man and hides the body under the floor; the officers come because a neighbour heard a shriek, the narrator confidently seats himself over the hiding place, hears the beating again, louder and louder, and unable to bear it confesses.
free_to_cut: repetitions of the narrator's arguments that he is wise and cunning, the old man's imagined thoughts and the personification of Death, the graphic details of how the body was dealt with, and the officers' formal introduction
source_essentials.narration_voice: The narrator speaks as 'I' (an unnamed first-person speaker) and keeps addressing the listener as 'you'; his calm, proud, over-confident voice, insisting that he is sane while he relishes his own cunning, is where the horror comes from.
